analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination against people with disabilities in jobs, public services, businesses, and phone service.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 76-8 and the House adopted the final deal 377-28, and the President signed it into law in July 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The Americans with Disabilities Act made it illegal to discriminate against people with disabilities in hiring, firing, and pay, and in services run by state and local governments. It required public transit, privately run businesses like stores and restaurants, and telephone companies to open their services to disabled Americans, including a 24-hour phone relay service for people who are deaf or have speech impairments. After both chambers passed it by overwhelming margins, it was signed into law on July 26, 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans with disabilities gain enforceable rights to equal treatment at work, on buses and trains, in stores, restaurants, hotels, and government offices, and over the telephone. Workers with conditions like HIV or epilepsy gain protection from being fired or screened out, though with some carve-outs. Employers also gain access to a much larger pool of workers and customers.

how_it_helps.text: Bans employers, unions, and employment agencies from discriminating against qualified people with disabilities in hiring, firing, pay, promotion, and training, and requires reasonable accommodation unless it would impose an undue burden.

Bars state and local governments from excluding disabled people from their programs, and requires accessible public buses, paratransit for those who cannot use fixed routes, and at least one accessible car per train.

Opens privately run places of public accommodation — stores, restaurants, hotels, theaters — to disabled customers, with the Attorney General empowered to sue pattern violators and courts able to order changes and civil penalties.

Requires telephone companies to provide telecommunications relay services around the clock, at rates no higher than voice calls, so people who are deaf or have speech impairments can use the phone like anyone else.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers must pay for reasonable accommodations and, over time, accessible workplaces; state and local governments and transit agencies must buy accessible buses, run paratransit, and retrofit rail stations; businesses must make their premises accessible; and telephone companies must fund relay services, costs that flow partly to customers through rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, transit agencies, businesses, phone companies

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: employers must pay for accommodations, businesses must alter premises, transit agencies must buy accessible buses and retrofit stations, and phone carriers must fund 24-hour relay service — burdens that fall hardest on small operators.

The final law includes a food-handling exception: employers may refuse to assign workers with certain infectious diseases to food-handling jobs, a concession won by opponents in the closing days that leaves some job discrimination legal.

The law's protections do not cover everyone who faces stigma: current illegal drug users are excluded, as are homosexuality, bisexuality, and certain gender-related conditions from the definition of disability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are historic — enforceable civil rights in work, transportation, commerce, and communication for millions of Americans — while the costs are the ordinary price of accessibility that businesses and governments had been avoiding. The honest complaints are about the compromises: the food-handling carve-out and the exclusions written into the definition of disability leave gaps in coverage, and compliance costs land hardest on small employers. On balance this is one of the clearest cases of a law whose public benefits dwarf its costs.

outcome.mechanism: It swept through both chambers by lopsided votes, survived a last fight over a food-handling exception in a House-Senate conference, and was signed into law on July 26, 1990.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on May 9, 1989; the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee held hearings and reported it favorably with a substitute amendment that August.
The Senate passed it 76-8 on September 7, 1989 — all 55 Democrats and 32 of 45 Republicans in favor.
The House passed its own version under a rule in May 1990, then requested a conference, and the two chambers negotiated a combined bill through June and July 1990.

A last-ditch motion by Representative Dannemeyer to send the deal back with instructions to let employers bar people with infectious diseases from food-handling jobs failed 180-224 on July 12, 1990; the House then adopted the conference report 377-28.
The Senate agreed to the final deal 91-6 on July 13, and the President signed it into law on July 26, 1990, as Public Law 101-336.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with disabilities came out ahead, gaining the country's broadest civil rights protections since the 1960s. Employers also came out ahead in the compromises: the food-handling exception, the business-necessity defense, and the exclusions of drug users and certain conditions from coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with disabilities; employers won carve-outs

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelming in both parties: the Senate passed it 76-8 (44-0 among Democrats, 32-8 among Republicans), and the final conference report won 91-6 in the Senate and 377-28 in the House (232-5 among House Democrats, 145-23 among House Republicans); the main resistance was a mostly-Republican faction, 124 of 175 House Republicans plus 56 Democrats, backing the failed food-handling exception.

industries.note: The law imposes duties to accommodate disabled workers and job applicants, which business groups resisted. It also opens a larger pool of workers and customers, but the immediate interest — minimizing accommodation and liability costs — ran against the disability community's push for strong coverage.

They must buy accessible buses, run paratransit for riders who cannot use fixed routes, and retrofit key rail stations, with extensions available only for extraordinarily expensive structural changes. Those costs are exactly what disabled riders had been denied for decades.

Every common carrier must provide 24-hour relay services for deaf and speech-impaired callers at rates no higher than voice service, spreading the cost across the phone system. Their cost burden is the public's access.

They must accommodate disabled workers and customers, but the last-minute food-handling exception lets them reassign workers with certain infectious diseases away from food handling. That carve-out came at the expense of workers with conditions like HIV.
New accessible-design requirements and retrofit mandates created steady demand for accessible construction and design work. The industry's interest ran alongside the public's here.
